'''''Eucalyptus melliodora''''', commonly known as '''yellow box''', '''honey box''' or '''yellow ironbox''',<ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus melliodora'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_melliodora.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=31 May 2020}}</ref> is a species of medium-sized to occasionally tall tree that is [[Endemism|endemic]] to south-eastern, continental Australia. It has rough, flaky or fibrous bark on part or all of the trunk, smooth greyish to yellowish bark above. The adult leaves are lance-shaped to egg-shaped, the flower buds are arranged in groups of seven and the fruit is more or less hemispherical.

==Description==
''Eucalyptus melliodora'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|30|m}} and forms a [[lignotuber]]. The bark is variable ranging from smooth with an irregular, short stocking, to covering most of the trunk, fibrous, dense or loosely held, grey, yellow or red-brown, occasionally very coarse, thick, dark brown to black. The smooth bark above is shed from the upper limbs to leave a smooth, white or yellowish surface. Young plants and [[coppice]] regrowth have lance-shaped to elliptic leaves that are {{cvt|25-65|mm}} long and {{cvt|9-35|mm}} wide and [[Petiole (botany)|petiolate]]. Adult leaves are the same dull light green or slate grey on both surfaces, lance-shaped to egg-shaped, {{cvt|60-140|mm}} long and {{cvt|8-30|mm}} wide on a petiole {{cvt|8-20|mm}} long. The vein on the leaf margin of both adult and juvenile leaves is markedly distant from the leaf margin.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus melliodora'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20melliodora |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra. |access-date=3 November 2019}}</ref><ref>Brooker & Kleinig, Eucalyptus, An illustrated guide to identification, Reed Books, Melbourne, 1996</ref>

The flower buds are arranged in groups of seven on an unbranched [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|3-10|mm}} long, the individual buds on [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] {{cvt|2-10|mm}} long. Mature buds are club-shaped, oval or diamond-shaped, {{cvt|4-8|mm}} long and {{cvt|3-5|mm}} wide with a conical to rounded [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. Flowering has been recorded in most months and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody, hemispherical to shortened spherical [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|3-8|mm}} long and {{cvt|3-7|mm}} wide with the fruit near or below rim level.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="ABRS" />

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Eucalyptus melliodora'' was first formally described in 1843 by [[Johannes Conrad Schauer]] from an unpublished description by [[Allan Cunningham (botanist)|Allan Cunningham]] and the description was published in [[Wilhelm Gerhard Walpers|Walpers']] book ''Repertorium Botanices Systematicae''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus melliodora''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455668|publisher=APNI|access-date=3 November 2019}}</ref><ref name="Schauer">{{cite book |editor-last1=Walpers |editor-first1=Wilhelm Gerhard |last1=Schauer |first1=Johannes Conrad |title=Repertorium Botanices Systematicae (Volume 2) |date=1843 |location=New York |page=924 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/32093#page/940/mode/1up |access-date=3 November 2019}}</ref> The [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] (''melliodora'') is derived from the Latin words ''melleus'' meaning "honey" and ''odorus'' "scented".<ref name="CANBR" /> There a number of common names applied to ''E. melliodora'' including: Yellow Box, Yellow Ironbox, Yellow Jacket, Yellow Ironbark, Dargan, Honey Box and Honey-scented Gum as detailed in the Australian National Species List.<ref name="auNSL">{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus melliodora''|url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/rest/name/apni/99652/api/apni-format|publisher=auNSL, Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=14 May 2026}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Yellow box is widely distributed on the eastern plains and tablelands from western [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]], [[New South Wales]] and up from the [[Canberra|capital territory]] to south-central [[Queensland]].<ref>{{cite book |title= Trees of Victoria |author=Costermans, L.F. |year=1981 |publisher= Author |location=Melbourne |isbn=0-9599105-1-4 }}</ref>

==Ecology==
It is associated with inland grey box, fuzzy box (''[[Eucalyptus conica|E. conica]]''), white box (''[[Eucalyptus albens|E. albens]]''), pilliga grey box (''[[Eucalyptus pilligaensis|E. pilligaensis]]''), red ironbark (''[[Eucalyptus sideroxylon|E. sideroxylon]]''), narrow-leaved ironbark (''[[Eucalyptus crebra|E. crebra]]''), Blakely's red gum (''[[Eucalyptus blakelyi|E. blakelyi]]''), apple species (''[[Angophora]]''), black cypress (''[[Callitris endlicheri]]''), white cypress (''[[Callitris glaucophylla]]''), kurrajong (''[[Brachychiton populneus]]'') and wattles (''[[Acacia]]'') species.<ref name=Boland2006>{{Cite book| last1= Boland | first1= Douglas J. | last2= Brooker | first2= M. Ian H. | author-link2= Ian Brooker | last3= Chippendale | first3= G. M. | last4= McDonald | first4= Maurice W. | title= Forest trees of Australia| publisher= CSIRO Publishing| location= Collingwood, Victoria| year= 2006| page= 464| isbn= 0-643-06969-0| url= https://books.google.com/books?id=q2v3kb9tFsYC&q=%22Eucalyptus+albens%22&pg=PA463 }}</ref>

==Uses==
''Eucalyptus melliodora'' provides good firewood and hard, strong, durable timber. The honey produced from it is renowned for its quality.<ref name="Eucalypts">{{cite book |last1=Kelly |first1=Stan |last2=Chippendale |first2=George M. |last3=Johnston |first3=R.D. |title=Eucalypts |date=1983 |volume=1|isbn=0-17-006257-0 |page=65|publisher=Nelson }}</ref>

==Notable specimens==
One of the few trees to [[Hibakujumoku|survive]] the blast from the 6 August 1945 atomic bombing of [[Hiroshima]] Japan, was an ''E. melliodora''. The tree was located {{cvt|740|m}} from the hypocenter, and as of April 2019 was still standing.<ref name="UNITAR">{{cite web |title=Database of ''Hibaku Jumoku'' ― Atomic-Bombed Trees of Hiroshima |url=http://www.unitar.org/hiroshima/sites/unitar.org.hiroshima/files/A-bombed%20trees%20worddoc%20as%20of%20Dec.%202011_1.pdf |publisher=[[United Nations Institute for Training and Research]] |access-date=27 May 2020 |archive-date=29 March 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170329060433/http://www.unitar.org/hiroshima/sites/unitar.org.hiroshima/files/A-bombed%20trees%20worddoc%20as%20of%20Dec.%202011_1.pdf |url-status=bot: unknown }}</ref>
